overview.text: The Kingdom of Portugal developed from a medieval polity on the western Iberian Peninsula. Portugal's government dates its founding to 1143, while its monarchy ended with the establishment of a republic in 1910. During the late fifteenth century, Portuguese navigators found a sea route around Africa's Cape of Good Hope, opening direct European maritime contact with the Indian Ocean. Vasco da Gama's voyage reached Calicut in India in 1498. Portuguese merchants then built trading links in India and China, including Macau. Overseas commerce, conquest, and missionary activity made the kingdom a major participant in early modern global exchange. The kingdom's history therefore connects European state formation with maritime exploration and empire.

The Portuguese monarchy ended when a republic was established in 1910.

overview.text: The Cultural Revolution was a political and social campaign launched by Mao Zedong in China in 1966 and conventionally dated through 1976. Mao appealed especially to young people organized as Red Guards, who attacked supposed enemies of the revolution and symbols labeled old or bourgeois. Party officials, teachers, and intellectuals faced public criticism, removal, and persecution, while schools and institutions were disrupted. The campaign was also a struggle over power within the Chinese Communist Party, including attacks on officials Mao regarded as opponents. Its most intense early phase came in the late 1960s, but the wider period continued until Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976. Its human and cultural costs were immense.

Mao Zedong mobilized young Red Guards during the campaign.
Red Guards attacked party officials and things they called old or counterrevolutionary.

overview.text: Māori are the Indigenous Polynesian people of Aotearoa New Zealand. Their ancestors voyaged from East Polynesia and settled the islands by about 1300 CE, though the exact timing remains debated. Māori communities developed distinct iwi, or tribes, and hapū, or subtribes, with strong ties to land, ancestry, and language. European trade introduced muskets, which became part of intertribal conflicts known as the Musket Wars in the early nineteenth century. In 1840, many Māori rangatira signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi with representatives of the British Crown; others did not. Its Māori and English texts differ in important ways, especially over governance and chiefly authority, and those differences remain central to New Zealand history.

Current scholarship places initial settlement around the late 1200s or by 1300 CE.
Iwi are tribes and hapū are subtribes or related community groups.

overview.text: The Trojan War is a legendary conflict in which an alliance of Greek forces besieged Troy, a city in Anatolia. In the traditional story, Paris of Troy takes Helen from Sparta, prompting her husband Menelaus and other Greek leaders to launch an expedition. Homer's Iliad focuses on a short stretch of the war, especially the quarrel of Achilles and the death of the Trojan champion Hector; it does not tell the entire story. Later traditions describe the Greeks hiding warriors inside a wooden horse, which the Trojans bring into their city. The tale shaped ancient literature and art. Archaeologists have found remains of a real city at Troy, but no single historical war can be identified with certainty as the epic's source.

Tradition connects the conflict to Paris taking Helen from Menelaus.
Homer’s Iliad narrates only a portion of the war, centered on Achilles and Hector.
In the wooden-horse story, hidden Greek warriors enter Troy by deception.
The historical basis of the epic war remains uncertain.

overview.text: The First Council of Nicaea met in 325 CE in Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Emperor Constantine summoned Christian bishops amid a dispute over Arius's teaching about the relationship between Jesus Christ and God the Father. The bishops produced an early form of the Nicene Creed and rejected Arius's position. In the council's formula, the Son was described as 'begotten, not made' and of the same substance as the Father. It is called the first ecumenical council because bishops from across the church were invited to deliberate on a common issue. A later council at Constantinople in 381 expanded the creed familiar to many Christians today.

Its creed described the Son as “begotten, not made” and of the same substance as the Father.

overview.text: Ford Motor Company is an American automobile maker founded by Henry Ford and partners in 1903. Its Model T, introduced in 1908, became closely associated with affordable motoring and large-scale production. Beginning in 1913, Ford's Highland Park plant used a moving assembly line to build cars more quickly; Ford did not invent the automobile itself. The company's history also reaches beyond Michigan. In the late 1920s it created Fordlândia along Brazil's Tapajós River, aiming to grow rubber for tires and reduce reliance on outside suppliers. The project faced major difficulties and did not become the dependable rubber source Ford hoped for. Model T production and Fordlândia show both the reach and limits of industrial planning.

key_facts.text: Henry Ford and partners founded Ford Motor Company in 1903.
The Model T was introduced in 1908.
Ford began using a moving automobile assembly line at Highland Park in 1913.
Fordlândia was a Ford rubber-plantation project in Brazil.
The Brazilian project aimed to supply rubber for automobile tires.

overview.text: Rishi Sunak is a British Conservative politician who served as Chancellor of the Exchequer from February 2020 to July 2022 and as prime minister from 25 October 2022 to 5 July 2024. He entered the House of Commons in 2015 as the member for Richmond (Yorks). His treasury role placed him in charge of the United Kingdom's finance ministry during the COVID-19 pandemic. After Boris Johnson and then Liz Truss left office in 2022, Sunak became prime minister and leader of the Conservative Party. He left the premiership after the 2024 general election and served briefly as leader of the opposition.

overview.text: Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, was a statesman of Piedmont-Sardinia who helped bring about Italian unification. As the kingdom's prime minister, he used diplomacy and alliances alongside military pressure against Austrian influence in northern Italy. Piedmont-Sardinia's participation in the Crimean War gave Cavour a place in European diplomacy, and in 1858 he met Napoleon III at Plombières to discuss French support against Austria. His plans at that stage did not yet amount to a single unified Italy; events moved beyond his initial proposals. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II became king of the new Kingdom of Italy, with Cavour as its first prime minister. Cavour died later that year, before Rome became the kingdom's capital.

overview.text: The Falklands War was fought in 1982 between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, known in Spanish as the Islas Malvinas. Argentina had long claimed sovereignty, while Britain administered the islands. Argentine forces landed on 2 April, and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's government sent a naval task force to regain control. British forces landed on East Falkland in May and advanced toward Port Stanley. Argentine troops surrendered there on 14 June, ending the 74-day conflict and restoring British administration. The fighting involved naval, air, and land operations and caused deaths on both sides. The sovereignty dispute continued afterward, so the military outcome did not settle every political question about the islands.

overview.text: Pancho Villa, born Doroteo Arango, was a military leader in the Mexican Revolution. He joined Francisco Madero's movement against the long rule of Porfirio Díaz and later commanded the powerful División del Norte, or Division of the North. Villa's forces fought the regime of Victoriano Huerta, but revolutionary alliances fractured after Huerta fell. In March 1916, Villa and his men attacked Columbus, New Mexico, prompting the United States to send General John J. Pershing into Mexico on a punitive expedition. That expedition failed to capture Villa. He eventually left armed struggle, and he was assassinated in 1923.
